explanations.explanation: Samuel, Israel's leader, appoints his sons as judges over Israel (1 Samuel 8:1). It's the family business, friend. I know that move, because I've handed my stamping to somebody else and watched with my mustache crossed. I think that's a lot to lay on two guys.
Servants don't show up in this verse at all. Samuel, Israel's leader, appoints his sons as judges over Israel. The text keeps it in the family, so the servants can stay in the kitchen.
No brothers in this verse, friend. When Samuel, Israel's leader, grows old, he appoints his sons as judges over Israel. It's the next generation getting the job, not the same generation.

Hold on, friend, the text says the opposite. “But his sons did not walk in his ways; they turned aside toward dishonest gain, accepting bribes and perverting justice.” (1 Samuel 8:3) Joel and Abijah took a different road than their dad. Samuel's name was on the sign, but the way they judged wasn't his.
That's right. The text says Samuel's sons “…did not walk in his ways…” (1 Samuel 8:3). They turned aside toward dishonest gain instead. A name on the sign doesn't make the cookies taste the same.

explanations.answer: They accept bribes and pervert justice
explanations.explanation: Yes, the text says they turned aside toward dishonest gain, “…accepting bribes and perverting justice.” (1 Samuel 8:3) Picture a judge whose ruling goes to the highest bidder. Nobody walks into that courtroom feeling like a winner unless they pay up.

explanations.answer: They stop holding court at all
explanations.explanation: The text never says they stopped holding court. Joel and Abijah were judges in Beersheba (1 Samuel 8:2). The text says they accepted bribes and perverted justice (1 Samuel 8:3). That's the trouble it names.

explanations.answer: They hand the land to the Philistines
explanations.explanation: Nothing in this passage says that. The Philistines, whom Israel went out to meet in battle (1 Samuel 4:1), don't come up here. The text says the sons took bribes and perverted justice (1 Samuel 8:3). That's a problem right inside the courtroom.

Right. The elders say, “Now appoint a king to judge us like all the other nations.” (1 Samuel 8:5) They point to Samuel being old and his sons not walking in his ways. Then comes the big ask, and it's a big one.

That's not what they ask for. The elders tell Samuel, “Now appoint a king to judge us like all the other nations.” (1 Samuel 8:5) They're not asking for a swap of judges. They want a whole different kind of leader.

explanations.answer: A new high priest for them
explanations.explanation: Nobody's asking for a new priest, friend. The elders say, “Now appoint a king to judge us like all the other nations.” (1 Samuel 8:5) That's a job posting for a king, and a priest isn't anywhere in it.

Not quite. The text says their demand was displeasing in Samuel's sight, and then it says, “so he prayed to the LORD.” (1 Samuel 8:6) No storming, no slammed door. I'd probably have thrown my hat on the floor, but Samuel took it to God.
That's right. The demand displeased Samuel, “so he prayed to the LORD.” (1 Samuel 8:6) The text says nothing about him storming out. When something stings, taking it to the LORD first is a good move.

Yes. The LORD says, “For it is not you they have rejected, but they have rejected Me as their king.” (1 Samuel 8:7) Samuel was the one standing there taking the ask. But the LORD says it was Him they were rejecting. That puts the whole request in a different light.
Eli isn't mentioned in this verse. Eli was a priest (1 Samuel 1:9). The LORD says, “…they have rejected Me as their king.” (1 Samuel 8:7) He's talking about Himself.

Moses, who led Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10), isn't in this verse. The LORD tells Samuel, “…it is not you they have rejected, but they have rejected Me as their king.” (1 Samuel 8:7) He names Himself. So the answer sits with the LORD.

That's right. The LORD says they have done this “…from the day I brought them up out of Egypt until this day, forsaking Me and serving other gods…” (1 Samuel 8:8) It's a long stretch, and He names it plainly. Then He says they're doing the same thing to Samuel.

The text says it's true, friend. The LORD says they have done this “…from the day I brought them up out of Egypt until this day, forsaking Me and serving other gods…” (1 Samuel 8:8) He's not talking about one bad week. He's looking at the whole stretch.

explanations.answer: Warn them what their king will be like
explanations.explanation: Yes. The LORD says, “…you must solemnly warn them and show them the manner of the king who will reign over them.” (1 Samuel 8:9) Samuel listens, and then he warns them. It's like reading all the fine print out loud before anyone signs.

explanations.answer: Have them fast and pray for forty days
explanations.explanation: Nothing about fasting or forty days is in this passage. The LORD tells Samuel to listen to their voice, then to “…solemnly warn them and show them the manner of the king who will reign over them.” (1 Samuel 8:9) The next job is a warning, so that's the one Samuel gets.

explanations.answer: Pick the king from his own family
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. The LORD tells Samuel to listen to the people, then to “…solemnly warn them and show them the manner of the king who will reign over them.” (1 Samuel 8:9) Nothing about picking from Samuel's family. The warning comes first.

explanations.answer: Put them to work for his chariots and horses
explanations.explanation: Yes. Samuel says, “He will take your sons and appoint them to serve his own chariots and horses, and to run in front of his chariots.” (1 Samuel 8:11) Running in front of a chariot is not a job with a comfortable chair. Samuel starts the list there, and it keeps going.

explanations.answer: Send them to study under the priests
explanations.explanation: Studying under the priests isn't in the warning. Samuel says the king “…will take your sons and appoint them to serve his own chariots and horses, and to run in front of his chariots.” (1 Samuel 8:11) These sons are going to work for the king. It's a job, not a classroom.

explanations.answer: Give each of them land of their own
explanations.explanation: Samuel says the opposite kind of thing. The king “…will take your sons and appoint them to serve his own chariots and horses, and to run in front of his chariots.” (1 Samuel 8:11) The word is take, and nobody is handing out land here. It's a warning, not a gift basket.

That's right. Samuel says, “And he will take your daughters to be perfumers, cooks, and bakers.” (1 Samuel 8:13) Bakers made the list, and I felt that one personally. Samuel says “He will take…” so it's the king doing the taking.
Weavers, potters and shepherds aren't on the list. Samuel says the king “…will take your daughters to be perfumers, cooks, and bakers.” (1 Samuel 8:13) That's three jobs, and it's a short list.
No singers or dancers in this warning. Samuel says the king “…will take your daughters to be perfumers, cooks, and bakers.” (1 Samuel 8:13) That's three jobs, and not one of them is a performance.

Yes. Samuel says the king “…will take a tenth of your grain and grape harvest and give it to his officials and servants.” (1 Samuel 8:15) Think of a paycheck that gets trimmed before it reaches you. In this case the king's own people get it.

Samuel doesn't say that. The king “…will take a tenth of your grain and grape harvest and give it to his officials and servants.” (1 Samuel 8:15) The tenth goes to the palace crowd. Priests and Levites aren't in the line.

That would be a different warning, friend. Samuel says the king will take a tenth of the grain and grape harvest “…and give it to his officials and servants.” (1 Samuel 8:15) The harvest ends up with the king's own people. The poor and widows aren't mentioned.

Yes, and it's the hardest line of the list. Samuel says, “He will take a tenth of your flocks, and you yourselves will become his slaves.” (1 Samuel 8:17) The fields, the animals, the harvest, and then the people themselves. Samuel gives the whole picture before they decide.
The text says it's true. Samuel says, “…you yourselves will become his slaves.” (1 Samuel 8:17) He saves the heaviest line for the end of the list. It's a hard thing to hear.

Samuel says the opposite, friend. He says, “When that day comes, you will beg for relief from the king you have chosen, but the LORD will not answer you on that day.” (1 Samuel 8:18) It's a sober line. The people are told ahead of time.

That's right. Samuel says, “…you will beg for relief from the king you have chosen, but the LORD will not answer you on that day.” (1 Samuel 8:18) Notice it says the king they have chosen. Samuel says it plainly, and it's a heavy moment.

explanations.answer: They refuse to listen to Samuel
explanations.explanation: Yes. The text says, “Nevertheless, the people refused to listen to Samuel.” Then they say, “No!” and “We must have a king over us.” (1 Samuel 8:19) Samuel just read out the full warning. They heard it and still said no.

explanations.answer: They ask Samuel for more time
explanations.explanation: They don't ask for time. The text says, “Nevertheless, the people refused to listen to Samuel.” (1 Samuel 8:19) Their answer is “No!” right away. They stay firm on their request.

explanations.answer: They ask Samuel to be their king
explanations.explanation: That's not what they say. They tell Samuel, “No!… We must have a king over us.” (1 Samuel 8:19) The people don't ask Samuel to take the job. They hold to the king they asked for.

explanations.answer: Go out before them and fight their battles
explanations.explanation: Yes. The people say they want “…a king to judge us, to go out before us, and to fight our battles.” (1 Samuel 8:20) That's the king they picture, going out before them and fighting. Samuel has just told them what that king will take.

explanations.answer: Build them a great temple in the city
explanations.explanation: A temple isn't in their request. They say they want “…a king to judge us, to go out before us, and to fight our battles.” (1 Samuel 8:20) The ask is about judging and leading in battle. Building doesn't come up.

explanations.answer: Bring the ark back to their camp
explanations.explanation: The ark isn't part of what they say. They tell Samuel they want “…a king to judge us, to go out before us, and to fight our battles.” (1 Samuel 8:20) Their words are about a king who judges and fights. That's the whole list.

The text says the opposite. After Samuel repeats the people's words, the LORD says, “Listen to their voice… Appoint a king for them.” (1 Samuel 8:22) He doesn't tell Samuel to refuse. The answer is a clear yes to the king.

That's right. The LORD tells Samuel, “Listen to their voice… Appoint a king for them.” (1 Samuel 8:22) Samuel took every word back to Him, and that's the answer he got. Then Samuel tells the men of Israel to go back to their cities.
